simulations.title: Pendulum Lab
simulations.subject: physics
simulations.summary: Explore how length, mass, gravity, and damping affect a pendulum's period. Drag the bob to set the angle, or use the slider.

controls.text: Drag coefficient — 0.00 is an ideal pendulum, 0.47 is a real sphere in air, 0.94 is double air drag.
Linear damping — extra friction proportional to speed. Leave at 0.00 for pure air drag.

cards.title: Period of a Pendulum
paragraphs: For small angles (< 15°), the period depends only on length and gravity — not on mass or amplitude. This is isochronism .

cards.title: Energy Dynamics
paragraphs: Energy transitions smoothly between Kinetic (K) and Potential (P). Air drag continuously dissipates mechanical energy into Thermal energy, so the Total line stays flat even as the pendulum slows.

cards.title: Large-Angle Correction
paragraphs: For angles above ~15°, the small-angle approximation breaks down. The true period increases slightly with amplitude.

cards.title: Explore
paragraphs: Try this: Set the drag coefficient to C _d = 0.00 for an ideal, non-damped pendulum and watch K and P swap forever with a flat Total line. Raise it to 0.47 (a real sphere in air) or 0.94 (twice normal air drag) to watch Thermal climb while Total stays flat — energy is conserved, just converted.
Drag the bob to change the angle. Change gravity to see how a pendulum would swing on the Moon (1.6 m/s²) or Jupiter (24.8 m/s²).

lessons.title: What controls a pendulum’s period?
lessons.summary: Predict, then measure how string length changes the time for one full swing.
lessons.subject: Physics

steps.title: A question first
steps.body:
The **period** T is the time for one full back-and-forth swing.

The string is 1.00 m long and the pendulum is paused. Before we measure anything, make a prediction.

steps.title: Your prediction
steps.body: If the string is **longer**, what happens to the period?

choices.label: A longer string gives a longer period
A longer string gives a shorter period

feedback.correct: Good — we will test that. The theory says T ≈ 2π√(L/g).
feedback.any: Keep your prediction in mind; you will measure it in a moment.

steps.title: Set the length to 2.00 m
steps.body: Use the **L** slider (or the arrow keys) until it reads 2.00 m.
steps.hint: The slider is the row labelled L.

steps.title: Release the pendulum
steps.body: Press **Resume** and let it swing. The simulation will time the period for you.

steps.title: Watch the period settle
steps.body: Let it swing for a few cycles. The highlighted **Period** readout converges once a full swing has been timed.

steps.title: You tested it
steps.body:
With drag removed, L = 1.00 m gives a period near **2.0 s**, while L = 2.00 m gives near **2.8 s**.

The period grows with the **square root** of the length — and, as you can check by changing mass, it does not depend on the bob’s mass.

questions.prompt: For an ideal small-angle pendulum, increasing length while keeping gravity fixed makes the period…
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(L/g). A longer pendulum takes longer to complete one full back-and-forth swing.

questions.prompt: With no drag, at small angles, doubling the bob mass while keeping length and gravity fixed makes the period…
questions.explanation: Mass cancels from the ideal pendulum equation. It is absent from T = 2π√(L/g); this claim assumes no drag.

questions.prompt: The same ideal small-angle pendulum is moved to a place with weaker gravity. Its period will…
questions.explanation: T is proportional to 1/√g. Weaker gravity gives a longer period, with length held fixed.

questions.prompt: If length is multiplied by four at fixed gravity, what happens to the ideal small-angle period?
questions.explanation: The square root of four is two. Period scales with √L, not directly with L.

questions.prompt: Which changes increase the period of an ideal small-angle pendulum? Hold other variables fixed for each change.
questions.explanation: In the small-angle approximation, only L and g set the period: increasing L or decreasing g increases T. Mass and small amplitude do not appear in this approximation.

choices.label: A very heavy bob is required

questions.explanation: The formula describes an ideal, small-angle pendulum. At large angles the period increases with amplitude; a heavy bob is not a requirement.

simulations.title: Circuit Builder
simulations.subject: physics
simulations.summary: Drag batteries, wires, switches, bulbs and resistors onto the board, snap them together, and watch the current flow.

controls.text: Select a part to edit it, or drag a part onto the board.
⚠ Short circuit! Current is flowing through a loop with no resistance. Add a resistor or bulb, or open a switch.
Pick a part, then drag on the board to place it. Drag the ends of a wire to snap it onto another part.

cards.title: Ohm's Law
paragraphs: Voltage (V) equals current (I) times resistance (R). It is the relationship behind every circuit you build here.

cards.title: Series Circuits
paragraphs: Parts in a single loop share one current. Resistances add up, and the voltage splits between the parts.

cards.title: Parallel Circuits
paragraphs: Parts side by side share the same voltage. The current splits between the branches and Req is smaller than any branch.

cards.title: Power
paragraphs: Energy per second. A bulb lights up in proportion to the power it dissipates, so a brighter bulb means more current.

cards.title: How To Use
paragraphs: Drag a part from the toolbox onto the board, or pick a tool and drag on the board to draw the part. Join two parts by dragging one end dot onto the other — a grey dot appears where they connect. Click a part to select it, then type an exact voltage or resistance in the box below the board (or double-click the part as a shortcut). Right-click, or use Erase, to remove a part.

simulations.title: Projectile Motion
simulations.subject: physics
simulations.summary: Launch a cannonball and explore projectile motion. Drag the cannon to reposition it, adjust angle and velocity, and watch the trajectory.

cards.title: Equations of Motion
paragraphs: Horizontal motion is constant velocity. Vertical motion is constant acceleration due to gravity (g = 9.8 m/s²).

cards.title: Components
paragraphs: The initial velocity vector is split into horizontal and vertical components using the launch angle.

cards.title: Key Quantities
paragraphs: Range = (v² sin(2θ)) / g (level ground) Max height = y _0 + (v _y ²) / (2g) Time of flight depends on launch height and vertical velocity.

cards.title: Tips
paragraphs: Drag the cannon anywhere on the canvas. Change the angle to see how 45° gives the longest range on level ground. Add height to clear obstacles.

questions.prompt: On level ground, a projectile launched at 60° has the same range as one launched at which angle?
questions.explanation: 30° — Correct! Complementary angles (summing to 90°) produce the same range on level ground. 60° + 30° = 90°, so they have equal range.

questions.prompt: On level ground, if you double launch speed while keeping the angle fixed, the range will:
questions.explanation: Quadruple — Correct! Range ∝ v² (R = v² sin(2θ) / g). Doubling v makes R four times larger.

questions.prompt: What happens to the time of flight if you increase the launch height (keeping angle and speed the same)?
questions.explanation: It increases — Correct! A higher launch point means the projectile has farther to fall to reach the ground, so it stays in the air longer.

questions.prompt: At what launch angle are the horizontal and vertical components of velocity equal (ignoring the sign)?
questions.explanation: 45° — Correct! At 45°, cos(45°) = sin(45°) = √2/2, so v _x = v cos(θ) = v sin(θ) = v _y .

simulations.title: Titration Bench
simulations.subject: chemistry
simulations.summary: Mix an acid and a base, then open the tap and watch the pH curve take shape as the drops fall.

canvas.label: Titration bench with burette, flask and pH curve

controls.label: Which solution is in the burette?

buttons.label: Press & hold to open the tap

empty.text: Turn on Auto-record readings and a row is added to this table each time you let go of the tap.

cards.title: Running the Bench
paragraphs: The vessel already holds a measured portion of one solution, and the burette is topped up with the other. Squeeze the tap open to let drops fall and let go to pause. When the burette reaches the bottom the run stops on its own.

cards.title: Getting Sensible Volumes
formulas: volume at equivalence ≈ 25 mL × (concentration in vessel ÷ concentration in burette)
paragraphs: The equivalence volume scales with the ratio of the two concentrations. For a comfortable run, keep the solution in the burette roughly 1¼ to 5× as concentrated as the one in the vessel. The suggested ranges under each concentration box update to keep the jump on the chart.

cards.title: The Equivalence Point
paragraphs: The two solutions have reacted completely when the moles of acid equal the moles of base. The pH at that moment depends on what is left behind in solution.

cards.title: Choosing a Colour Indicator
paragraphs: Each indicator flips colour across a span of about two pH units. Pick one whose colour change lands on the vertical part of the curve, otherwise the colour change you see will not match the true equivalence point.

cards.title: About the Numbers
paragraphs: The pH is found by solving the full equilibrium relations — a quadratic away from the jump and a cubic across it — so dilute and very weak acids stay accurate instead of relying on the usual short-cut. Pairing a weak acid with a weak base is left out because it needs a quartic.

simulations.title: Gas Laws
simulations.subject: chemistry
simulations.summary: Explore the ideal gas law by adjusting pressure, volume, temperature, and the number of gas particles. Drag the piston to change volume.

cards.title: Ideal Gas Law
paragraphs: Relates pressure (P), volume (V), number of moles (n), temperature (T), and the gas constant (R = 0.0821 L.atm.mol ^-1 .K ^-1 ).

cards.title: Boyle's Law
paragraphs: At constant temperature and moles, pressure and volume are inversely proportional. Squeeze the gas (decrease V) and pressure goes up (increase P).

cards.title: Charles's Law
paragraphs: At constant pressure and moles, volume is proportional to temperature. Heat the gas (increase T) and it expands (increase V).

cards.title: Gay-Lussac's Law
paragraphs: At constant volume and moles, pressure is proportional to temperature. Heat the gas (increase T) and pressure rises (increase P).

cards.title: Avogadro's Law
paragraphs: At constant pressure and temperature, volume is proportional to the number of moles. More particles (increase n) take up more space (increase V).

boyle.title: Boyle's Law
boyle.explanation: At constant temperature and moles, the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional. When you squeeze a gas into a smaller space, its pressure increases proportionally.
boyle.detail: Boyle's law describes how pressure and volume relate at constant n and T: P ∝ 1/V. If you double the volume, pressure halves; if you halve the volume, pressure doubles. This assumes the gas behaves ideally (no intermolecular forces and point-mass particles).

charles.title: Charles's Law
charles.explanation: At constant pressure and moles, the volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature. Heating a gas causes it to expand; cooling causes it to contract.
charles.detail: Charles's law states that volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant n and P: V ∝ T. At absolute zero (0 K), the volume of an ideal gas would theoretically reach zero. This is why temperature must be measured in Kelvin.

gaylussac.title: Gay-Lussac's Law
gaylussac.explanation: At constant volume and moles, the pressure of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature. Heating a gas in a rigid container increases the pressure.
gaylussac.detail: Gay-Lussac's law describes the direct proportionality between pressure and absolute temperature at constant n and V: P ∝ T. This explains why aerosol cans warn against heating - the pressure inside can rise until the container fails.

avogadro.title: Avogadro's Law
avogadro.explanation: At constant pressure and temperature, the volume of a gas is proportional to the number of moles. More gas particles require more space at the same pressure.
avogadro.detail: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules: V ∝ n. At STP (0 °C, 1 atm), one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L.

simulations.title: States of Matter
simulations.subject: chemistry
simulations.summary: Heat and cool atoms & molecules to observe solid, liquid, and gas phases.

cards.title: How It Works
paragraphs: Drag the slider to heat or cool. Particles interact through intermolecular forces: solid at low temperatures, liquid between the melting and boiling points, and gas above the boiling point.

cards.title: About Phase Changes
paragraphs: During a phase change, temperature stays constant while energy is absorbed or released — this is latent heat , the energy needed to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.

simulations.title: Build a Nucleus
simulations.subject: physics
simulations.summary: Add protons and neutrons to build atomic nuclei. Explore stability, isotopes, and the chart of nuclides.

graphs.label: Chart of Nuclides
graphs.caption: Click a cell to select that isotope. Cells that are blank are nuclides that do not exist.
